summary: Deletes a named user account and every session it holds, from inside a cloud function, as the system. Cloud-only.
description: Delete User removes the `_User` row whose id you give it, and every `_Session` row belonging to it, with the authority of the server. Sessions go first and that ordering is deliberate: a deleted user whose sessions survived would leave tokens that resolve to a row the backend can no longer fetch. `sessionsRevoked` reports how many went, which is also the honest answer to 'was anybody actually signed in as them?'. `userId` is required — a blank one is a `failure`, never the deletion of whoever called.
whenToUse: In a cloud function that closes accounts: a moderation action, an account-deletion request the user made in your app, or the cleanup half of a provisioning job. There is no browser equivalent and there deliberately is not one.

ports.userId: Value; required. Which account to delete. A blank one is a `failure`; this node never falls back to the caller.
ports.remove: Signal (Do); deletes the account and its sessions. Nothing is deleted until this fires.
ports.sessionsRevoked: Value; how many sessions the deleted account held. Zero after `unchanged`.
ports.done: Signal; fires once the account and its sessions are gone.
ports.unchanged: Signal; fires when there is no user with this id. Not a failure — the post-condition already holds, so a moderation job re-run after a partial failure does not go red on its second pass.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the account could not be deleted, including when `userId` is blank.
ports.error: Value; why the last attempt failed.
ports.treatUnchangedAs: Edit-only enum; set it to Failure if 'that account was already gone' should stop the chain.

patterns: Wire `done` and `unchanged` to the same Response when the function's job is 'make sure this account is gone'. Both mean it is.
antiPatterns: Wiring a request parameter straight into `userId` on a function anyone may call. That is 'delete any account by id' with an HTTP endpoint in front of it — give the function a `call` rule (CWF-017) and check inside the graph that the caller is entitled to delete that particular account.
Expecting a blank `userId` to delete the caller's own account. It is a failure; read the caller's id from the Request node's `userId` output and wire it in explicitly, so the graph says what it does.
